passage:
Instructor's note, written by Samir.
Sangeeta, twenty, was in a practice lesson at a busy junction when an auto scraped the side mirror of the training car. She jumped out, shouted at the driver, and said she would "file a case and break his mirror". I asked her to stand on the kerb with me. Her hands were shaking. I said only, "Breathe in slowly, out slower. It's a scrape." After a minute her voice lowered.
We took photographs, exchanged details with the auto driver and left, and I told her the insurance office can sort out the rest. In the car she said, "I felt he had no respect for me, and I was late." Then she asked to drive the rest of the lesson.

qa.q: What did the auto scrape?
qa.a: The auto scraped the side mirror of the training car.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling after the auto scraped the mirror?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt disrespected, rushed and angry, which she said herself in the car.

qa.q: What steps helped settle the situation after Sangeeta shouted?
qa.a: She stood on the kerb, breathed slowly, photographed the scrape, exchanged details, left the scene and let the insurance office sort out the rest.

qa.q: How might the auto driver have felt when Sangeeta jumped out shouting?
qa.a: The auto driver was probably alarmed or defensive at being shouted at over a small scrape.

grounding: A driver hit by a small scrape shouts and threatens, and breathing, leaving the scene and letting insurance handle it prevents worse.

passage:
Friday. Rashmi's car kissed my bumper at the signal and I lost it. I honked, jumped out and shouted, "Learn to drive!" My heart was pounding and my face felt on fire. I was late for my exam and it seemed like she didn't care. Rashmi kept her window up, pointed at her phone, and stayed calm. That made me angrier.
Sitting in my car afterwards, I saw the scrape. It was small. I felt silly and also sick that I had said those things.
Next time: breathe, take photos, swap details, drive away, and let insurance do the work. Rashmi handled it better than I did.
Avni

qa.q: Where did Rashmi's car touch Avni's bumper?
qa.a: It touched Avni's bumper at the signal.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when jumping out to shout?
qa.a: Avni felt angry, rushed and disrespected, with a pounding heart, since Avni was late for an exam.

qa.q: What plan does Avni make for the next time this happens?
qa.a: Avni plans to breathe, take photos, swap details, drive away and let insurance do the work.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt during Avni's shouting?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt uneasy or alarmed but stayed calm, keeping the window up and pointing at the phone instead of shouting back.

grounding: A driver hit by a small scrape shouts, feeling disrespected and rushed, and later sees that breathing and insurance would have been better.

passage:
Workplace wellbeing note, Tuesday.
Nandini, 22, one of our new analysts, came to see me after an incident in the office parking lot yesterday. A colleague, Charu, reversing slowly, scraped Nandini's car door. Nandini jumped out, shouted, and slammed her hand on Charu's bonnet. Security had to step in.
Today she was ashamed. "I don't even know what happened. I felt so disrespected, and I was already late, and then I just exploded."
We talked about how anger in traffic comes fast: adrenaline, pride, feeling rushed. I asked what might have helped. She said, "Breathing. Walking away. Just taking a photo and exchanging numbers."
I suggested she apologise to Charu. She said she would do it at lunch.
Next step: Nandini asked for the details of our employee counselling service to learn ways to manage anger. I've shared them.

qa.q: What did Nandini slam her hand on?
qa.a: She slammed her hand on Charu's bonnet.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel today about the incident?
qa.a: Nandini felt ashamed, not understanding how she exploded after feeling disrespected and rushed.

qa.q: What could Nandini do differently next time?
qa.a: Breathe, walk away, take a photo and exchange details, letting the process handle the scrape instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Nandini shouted?
qa.a: Charu probably felt frightened and shaken, especially since the scrape was small and she was reversing slowly.

grounding: A note shows a young adult who shouted after a small scrape, felt disrespected and rushed, and learned that breathing and walking away prevent worse.

passage:
Monday night
I'm embarrassed writing this.
On the way home, a car scraped my bumper at the signal. Tiny scratch. I jumped out and started yelling at the driver, a guy my age, Siddharth. I said things I don't even say to my brother. He yelled back. People gathered. My heart was pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears.
Then an old auto driver said, "Beta, it's a scratch. Nobody is hurt. Why fight?"
I suddenly felt stupid. We exchanged numbers, took photos of both cars, and left. His insurance will handle it.
In the car, I shook for ten minutes. It was adrenaline, I think, and pride. I felt disrespected, and I was late.
Next time: breathe, photo, numbers, leave. Say less.
Ira

qa.q: What did the old auto driver say?
qa.a: He said, "Beta, it's a scratch. Nobody is hurt. Why fight?"

qa.q: What was Ira feeling while yelling?
qa.a: Ira felt angry and disrespected, heart pounding, driven by adrenaline and pride.

qa.q: What does Ira plan to do next time, and why?
qa.a: Breathe, take photos, exchange numbers and leave, which prevents a small scrape from turning into something worse.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt during the argument?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt angry and defensive, which is why he yelled back.

grounding: A driver hit by a small scrape shouts in anger, then realises that breathing, exchanging details and leaving prevent worse.

passage: On the narrow market road in Margao, an auto-rickshaw scraped the side of Maria's car as it squeezed past. She jumped out, face burning. "Are you blind? Do you know what this costs?" The driver shouted back. A crowd gathered. Maria heard herself say, "I'll see you at the police station, you'll pay for every inch," and her fist was clenched. Her cousin Minakshi got out of the passenger seat and touched her elbow. "Maria. Breathe. Look at the scratch." It was a thin white line. Maria's heart was pounding. She was late for her exam form deadline, and the auto had a schoolchild in the back. Minakshi quietly photographed both number plates. "Insurance can handle it. Let's go." Maria got back in. Her hands shook on the wheel for two kilometres.

qa.q: What did Minakshi photograph?
qa.a: She photographed both number plates.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she jumped out of the car?
qa.a: Maria felt furious and disrespected, face burning and fist clenched, with the stress of being late adding to it.

qa.q: What calmed the situation, and why?
qa.a: Minakshi touched Maria's elbow, told her to breathe and look at the small scratch, took photos and suggested letting insurance handle it, so they could leave.

qa.q: What might the auto driver have been feeling with a schoolchild in the back?
qa.a: The driver was probably stressed and defensive, worried about the child and about being blamed, which is why the driver shouted back.

grounding: It illustrates a driver who shouts and threatens after a small scrape, and how breathing, leaving and letting insurance handle it prevent worse.
